findings.quote: Type Ia supernovae can be used as standard candles to measure extragalactic distances, which can in turn be used to measure how fast the universe has expanded in the past.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Data indicates the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate, the cause of which is usually ascribed to dark energy.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Since observations indicate the universe is almost flat, it is expected the total energy density of everything in the universe should sum to 1 (Ωtot ≈ 1).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The measured dark energy density is ΩΛ ≈ 0.690; the observed ordinary (baryonic) matter energy density is Ωb ≈ 0.0482 and the energy density of radiation is negligible.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This leaves a missing Ωdm ≈ 0.258 which nonetheless behaves like matter (see technical definition section above) – dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Although both dark matter and ordinary matter are matter, they do not behave in the same way.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: In particular, in the early universe, ordinary matter was ionized and interacted strongly with radiation via Thomson scattering.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Dark matter does not interact directly with radiation, but it does affect the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by its gravitational potential (mainly on large scales) and by its effects on the density and velocity of ordinary matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Ordinary and dark matter perturbations, therefore, evolve differently with time and leave different imprints on the CMB.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This is also the reason why neutrinos, which move at nearly the speed of light and therefore would fall under hot dark matter, cannot make up the bulk of dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: However, multiple lines of evidence suggest the majority of dark matter is not baryonic:
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Sufficient diffuse, baryonic gas or dust would be visible when backlit by stars.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: If there are more baryons, then there should also be more helium, lithium and heavier elements synthesized during the Big Bang.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: In contrast, large-scale structure and other observations indicate that the total matter density is about 30% of the critical density.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Detailed analysis of the small irregularities (anisotropies) in the cosmic microwave background by WMAP and Planck indicate that around five-sixths of the total matter is in a form that only interacts significantly with ordinary matter or photons through gravitational effects.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: There are two main candidates for non-baryonic dark matter: new particles and primordial black holes.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Unlike baryonic matter, nonbaryonic particles do not contribute to the formation of the elements in the early universe (Big Bang nucleosynthesis) and so its presence is felt only via its gravitational effects (such as weak lensing).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: There exists no formal definition of a Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP), but broadly, it is an elementary particle which interacts via gravity and any other force (or forces) which is as weak as or weaker than the weak nuclear force, but also non-vanishing in strength.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Many WIMP candidates are expected to have been produced thermally in the early Universe, similarly to the particles of the Standard Model according to Big Bang cosmology, and usually will constitute cold dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Because supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics readily predict a new particle with these properties, this apparent coincidence has been called the "WIMP miracle", and a stable supersymmetric partner has long been a prime explanation for dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Experimental efforts to detect WIMPs include the search for products of WIMP annihilation, including gamma rays, neutrinos and cosmic rays in nearby galaxies and galaxy clusters; direct detection experiments designed to measure the collision of WIMPs with nuclei in the laboratory, as well as attempts to directly produce WIMPs in colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider at CERN.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: In the early 2010s, results from direct-detection experiments along with the lack of evidence for supersymmetry at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiment have cast doubt on the simplest WIMP hypothesis.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Axions are hypothetical elementary particles originally theorized in 1978 independently by Frank Wilczek and Steven Weinberg as the Goldstone boson of Peccei–Quinn theory, which had been proposed in 1977 to solve the strong CP problem in quantum chromodynamics (QCD).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: QCD effects produce an effective periodic potential in which the axion field moves.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Expanding the potential about one of its minima, one finds that the product of the axion mass with the axion decay constant is determined by the topological susceptibility of the QCD vacuum.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: An axion with mass that is much less than 60 keV/c2 is long-lived and weakly interacting: a perfect dark matter candidate.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The oscillations of the axion field about the minimum of the effective potential, the so-called misalignment mechanism, generate a cosmological population of cold axions with an abundance depending on the mass of the axion.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: With a mass above 5 μeV/c2 (10−11 times the electron mass) axions could account for dark matter, and thus be both a dark-matter candidate and a solution to the strong CP problem.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: If inflation occurs at a low scale and lasts sufficiently long, the axion mass can be as low as 1 peV/c2.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothetical black holes that formed soon after the Big Bang.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: In the inflationary era and early radiation-dominated universe, extremely dense pockets of subatomic matter may have been tightly packed to the point of gravitational collapse, creating black holes without the supernova compression typically needed to create stellar black holes.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The idea was first suggested by Yakov Zeldovich and Igor Dmitriyevich Novikov in 1966, and independently by Stephen Hawking in 1971.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Because PBHs would form prior to stellar evolution, they are non-baryonic dark matter candidates and are not limited to the narrow mass range of stellar black holes; they could range from Planck-mass relics to supermassive scales.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Interest in PBHs as a primary component of dark matter was revived following the 2015 discovery of gravitational waves by LIGO.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Their first detected merger involved black holes of approximately 30 solar masses; such objects are difficult to explain via standard stellar collapse but fit the predicted mass range for PBHs formed during the QCD transition in the early universe.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This interest was bolstered in November 2025, when the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA collaboration reported a candidate gravitational wave signal from a sub-solar mass merger.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: As no astrophysical process is known to produce black holes below the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses), confirmed sub-solar mass objects would be strong evidence for a primordial origin.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: As there have been no gravitational waves detected at z>1 (>6 Gya), and the sensitivity to lower-mass collisions falls off with distance, we are not currently able to detect collisions in the earliest half of the age of the universe.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Further support for the PBH hypothesis has emerged from James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the high-redshift universe (z > 7).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: JWST discovered unexpected populations of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs, compact very high redshift objects) and "overmassive black hole galaxies" such as UHZ1 and GHZ2, which contain supermassive black holes appearing less than 500 million years after the Big Bang and outweighing their galaxy's stars.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: These active galactic nuclei challenge standard models of accretion from "light" stellar black hole seeds, and suggest "heavy seeds" formed via direct collapse or PBHs, which could account for a significant fraction of dark matter halos.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Various observational constraints, such as gravitational microlensing data from the Subaru Telescope (HSC) and from Voyager 1 electron-positron data have ruled out PBHs constituting 100% of dark matter in specific mass windows (e.g., evaporating tiny black holes or monochromatic intermediate-mass populations).

findings.quote: Consequently, producing the required abundance of PBHs typically necessitates "exotic" inflation models, often featuring inflection points, bumps, or plateaus in the inflaton potential, which can amplify fluctuations by orders of magnitude.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Critics argue that these models require significant fine-tuning, as the resulting PBH abundance is exponentially sensitive to the amplitude of these fluctuations; meaning that a slight deviation in parameters results in either a negligible amount of dark matter or a universe dominated entirely by black holes.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: by these exotic inflation models provide a unified explanation for observational anomalies seen by LIGO and JWST that particle models do not address.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: One such mechanism is the QCD phase transition; as the universe cooled through this epoch, the reduction in the equation of state (pressure) naturally lowered the threshold for gravitational collapse.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This effect automatically enhances the formation of black holes at the solar mass scale, comparable to those detected by gravitational wave observatories, without requiring a precisely tuned peak in the inflation power spectrum.

findings.quote: Additionally, models involving multiple scalar fields can produce sharp spikes in density fluctuations through dynamic interactions, such as rapid turns in the field trajectory, which derive the necessary conditions from the model's geometric structure rather than from fine-tuned parameters.

findings.quote: Indirect detection experiments search for the products of the self-annihilation or decay of dark matter particles in outer space.

findings.quote: For example, in regions of high dark matter density (e.g., the centre of the Milky Way) two dark matter particles could annihilate to produce gamma rays or Standard Model particle–antiparticle pairs.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: These processes could be detected indirectly through an excess of gamma rays, antiprotons or positrons emanating from high density regions in the Milky Way and other galaxies.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Thus dark matter may accumulate at the center of these bodies, increasing the chance of collision/annihilation.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The detection by LIGO in September 2015 of gravitational waves opens the possibility of observing dark matter in a new way, particularly if it is in the form of primordial black holes.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Beyond searching for annihilation products, astrophysicists are using celestial objects as natural detectors to constrain dark matter particle properties.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Stellar heating: If dark matter particles capture inside dense stars like neutron stars or white dwarfs, they can deposit kinetic energy during the capture process or through subsequent annihilation.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This mechanism, known as "dark kinetic heating", would maintain the star at a temperature higher than expected for its age, potentially arresting its cooling indefinitely.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The observation of old, "cold" neutron stars therefore places stringent limits on the scattering cross-section of dark matter particles with nucleons, as any significant interaction would have kept these stars hotter than observed.

findings.quote: If dark matter is not an undiscovered particle, then the next possibility is that general relativity, the theory underpinning modern cosmology, is incorrect.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: General relativity is well-tested on Solar System scales, but its validity on galactic or cosmological scales has not been well proven.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: A suitable modification to general relativity can conceivably eliminate the need for dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The best-known theories of this class are modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) and its relativistic generalization tensor–vector–scalar gravity (TeVeS), f(R) gravity, negative mass, dark fluid, entropic gravity, conformal gravity, and massive gravity.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Alternative theories abound.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: A problem with modifying gravity is that observational evidence for dark matter – let alone general relativity – comes from so many independent approaches (see § Observational evidence above).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Explaining any individual observation is possible but explaining all of them in the absence of dark matter is very difficult.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Nonetheless, there have been some scattered successes for alternative hypotheses, such as a 2016 test of gravitational lensing in entropic gravity and a 2020 measurement of a unique MOND effect.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The prevailing opinion among most astrophysicists is that while modifications to general relativity can conceivably explain part of the observational evidence, there is probably enough data to conclude there must be some form of dark matter present in the universe.

findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: They could be from dark matter annihilation or from pulsars.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: In 2013, results from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on the International Space Station indicated excess high-energy cosmic rays which could be due to dark matter annihilation.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The detection by LIGO in September 2015 of gravitational waves opens the possibility of observing dark matter in a new way, particularly if it is in the form of primordial black holes.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Beyond searching for annihilation products, astrophysicists are using celestial objects as natural detectors to constrain dark matter particle properties.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Stellar heating: If dark matter particles capture inside dense stars like neutron stars or white dwarfs, they can deposit kinetic energy during the capture process or through subsequent annihilation.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This mechanism, known as "dark kinetic heating", would maintain the star at a temperature higher than expected for its age, potentially arresting its cooling indefinitely.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The observation of old, "cold" neutron stars therefore places stringent limits on the scattering cross-section of dark matter particles with nucleons, as any significant interaction would have kept these stars hotter than observed.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: If dark matter is not an undiscovered particle, then the next possibility is that general relativity, the theory underpinning modern cosmology, is incorrect.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: General relativity is well-tested on Solar System scales, but its validity on galactic or cosmological scales has not been well proven.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: A suitable modification to general relativity can conceivably eliminate the need for dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The best-known theories of this class are modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) and its relativistic generalization tensor–vector–scalar gravity (TeVeS), f(R) gravity, negative mass, dark fluid, entropic gravity, conformal gravity, and massive gravity.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Alternative theories abound.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: A problem with modifying gravity is that observational evidence for dark matter – let alone general relativity – comes from so many independent approaches (see § Observational evidence above).
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Explaining any individual observation is possible but explaining all of them in the absence of dark matter is very difficult.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Nonetheless, there have been some scattered successes for alternative hypotheses, such as a 2016 test of gravitational lensing in entropic gravity and a 2020 measurement of a unique MOND effect.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The prevailing opinion among most astrophysicists is that while modifications to general relativity can conceivably explain part of the observational evidence, there is probably enough data to conclude there must be some form of dark matter present in the universe.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: While WIMPs, axions, and primordial black holes remain the primary candidates for dark matter, numerous other theories have been proposed to address specific observational anomalies or theoretical motivations.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: These alternative models often explore mass ranges and interaction strengths outside the standard parameter space, ranging from ultra-light scalar fields to massive composite states.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Some hypotheses posit the existence of complex "dark sectors" with their own fundamental forces, while others suggest that dark matter may be unstable, dynamical, or composed of mirror particles.

findings.quote: In astronomy and cosmology, baryonic dark matter is hypothetical dark matter composed of baryons.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Only a small proportion of the dark matter in the universe is likely to be baryonic.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: As "dark matter", baryonic dark matter is undetectable by its emitted radiation, but its presence can be inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This form of dark matter is composed of "baryons", heavy subatomic particles such as protons and neutrons and combinations of these, including non-emitting ordinary atoms.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Baryonic dark matter may occur in non-luminous gas or in Massive Astrophysical Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs) – condensed objects such as black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs, very faint stars, or non-luminous objects like planets and brown dwarfs.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: The total amount of baryonic dark matter can be inferred from models of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and observations of the cosmic microwave background.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Both indicate that the amount of baryonic dark matter is much smaller than the total amount of dark matter.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: From the perspective of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, a larger amount of ordinary (baryonic) matter implies a denser early universe, more efficient conversion of matter to helium-4, and less unburned deuterium remaining.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: If all of the dark matter in the universe were baryonic, then there would be much less deuterium in the universe than is observed.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Biological dark matter is an informal term for unclassified or poorly understood genetic material.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: This genetic material may refer to genetic material produced by unclassified microorganisms.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: By extension, biological dark matter may also refer to the un-isolated microorganisms whose existence can only be inferred from the genetic material that they produce.
findings.relevance: Reader-selected chunk; original text copied verbatim by code.

findings.quote: Some of the genetic material may not fall under the three existing domains of life: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota; thus, it has been suggested that a possible fourth domain of life may yet be discovered, although other explanations are also probable.

findings.quote: Alternatively, the genetic material may refer to non-coding DNA (so-called "junk DNA") and non-coding RNA produced by known organisms.

findings.quote: Uncategorized genetic material is found in humans and many other species.

C1S2.text: Dark matter is implied by gravitational effects that cannot be explained by general relativity unless more matter is present than can be observed.

C2S3.text: While the density of dark matter is significant in the halo around a galaxy, its local density in the Solar System is much less than normal matter.

C4S1.text: Although the astrophysics community generally accepts the existence of dark matter, a minority of astrophysicists, intrigued by specific observations that are not well explained by ordinary dark matter, argue for various modifications of the standard laws of general relativity.

C22S1.text: In standard cosmological calculations, "matter" means any constituent of the universe whose energy density scales with the inverse cube of the scale factor, i.e., ρ ∝ a−3 .
C22S1.title: Dark matter

C22S2.text: This is in contrast to "radiation", which scales as the inverse fourth power of the scale factor ρ ∝ a−4 , and a cosmological constant, which does not change with respect to a (ρ ∝ a0).
C22S2.title: Dark matter

C22S3.text: The different scaling factors for matter and radiation are a consequence of radiation redshift.
C22S3.title: Dark matter

C22S4.text: For example, after doubling the diameter of the observable Universe via cosmic expansion, the scale, a, has doubled.
C22S4.title: Dark matter

C22S5.text: The energy of the cosmic microwave background radiation has been halved (because the wavelength of each photon has doubled); the energy of ultra-relativistic particles, such as early-era standard-model neutrinos, is similarly halved.
C22S5.title: Dark matter

C22S6.text: The cosmological constant, as an intrinsic property of space, has a constant energy density
C22S6.title: Dark matter

C24S1.text: In principle, "dark matter" means all components of the universe which are not visible but still obey ρ ∝ a−3 .
C24S1.title: Dark matter

C24S2.text: In practice, the term "dark matter" is often used to mean only the non-baryonic component of dark matter, i.e., excluding "missing baryons".
C24S2.title: Dark matter

C24S3.text: Context will usually indicate which meaning is intended.
C24S3.title: Dark matter

C28S1.text: Galaxy clusters are particularly important for dark matter studies since their masses can be estimated in three independent ways:
C28S1.title: Dark matter

C29S1.text: From the scatter in radial velocities of the galaxies within clusters
C29S1.title: Dark matter

C30S1.text: From X-rays emitted by hot gas in the clusters.
C30S1.title: Dark matter

C30S2.text: From the X-ray energy spectrum and flux, the gas temperature and density can be estimated, hence giving the pressure; assuming pressure and gravity balance determines the cluster's mass profile.
C30S2.title: Dark matter

C31S1.text: Gravitational lensing (usually of more distant galaxies) can measure cluster masses without relying on observations of dynamics (e.g., velocity).
C31S1.title: Dark matter

C32S1.text: Generally, these three methods are in reasonable agreement that dark matter outweighs visible matter by approximately 5 to 1.
C32S1.title: Dark matter

C33S1.text: On larger scales, large galaxy redshift surveys may be used to make a three-dimensional map of the galaxy distribution.
C33S1.title: Dark matter

C33S2.text: These maps are slightly distorted because distances are estimated from observed redshifts; the redshift contains a contribution from the galaxy's so-called peculiar velocity in addition to the dominant Hubble expansion term.
C33S2.title: Dark matter

C33S3.text: On average, superclusters are expanding more slowly than the cosmic mean due to their gravity, while voids are expanding faster than average.
C33S3.title: Dark matter

C33S4.text: In a redshift map, galaxies in front of a supercluster have excess radial velocities towards it and have redshifts slightly higher than their distance would imply, while galaxies behind the supercluster have redshifts slightly low for their distance.
C33S4.title: Dark matter

C33S5.text: This effect causes superclusters to appear squashed in the radial direction, and likewise voids are stretched.
C33S5.title: Dark matter

C34S1.title: Dark matter

C34S2.text: It was predicted quantitatively by Nick Kaiser in 1987, and first decisively measured in 2001 by the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey.
C34S2.title: Dark matter

C34S3.text: Results are in agreement with the Lambda-CDM model.

C35S1.text: The bullet cluster is the result of a recent collision of two galaxy clusters.
C35S1.title: Dark matter

C35S2.text: It is of particular note because the location of the center of mass as measured by gravitational lensing is different from the location of the center of mass of visible matter.
C35S2.title: Dark matter

C35S3.text: This is difficult for modified gravity theories, which generally predict lensing around visible matter, to explain.
C35S3.title: Dark matter

C35S4.text: Standard dark matter theory however has no issue: the hot, visible gas in each cluster would be cooled and slowed down by electromagnetic interactions, while dark matter (which does not interact electromagnetically) would not.
C35S4.title: Dark matter

C35S5.text: This leads to the dark matter separating from the visible gas, producing the separate lensing peak as observed.
C35S5.title: Dark matter

C38S1.text: Type Ia supernovae can be used as standard candles to measure extragalactic distances, which can in turn be used to measure how fast the universe has expanded in the past.
C38S1.title: Dark matter

C38S2.text: Data indicates the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate, the cause of which is usually ascribed to dark energy.
C38S2.title: Dark matter

C38S3.text: Since observations indicate the universe is almost flat, it is expected the total energy density of everything in the universe should sum to 1 (Ωtot ≈ 1).
C38S3.title: Dark matter

C38S4.text: The measured dark energy density is ΩΛ ≈ 0.690; the observed ordinary (baryonic) matter energy density is Ωb ≈ 0.0482 and the energy density of radiation is negligible.
C38S4.title: Dark matter

C38S5.text: This leaves a missing Ωdm ≈ 0.258 which nonetheless behaves like matter (see technical definition section above) – dark matter.
C38S5.title: Dark matter

C40S1.text: Although both dark matter and ordinary matter are matter, they do not behave in the same way.
C40S1.title: Dark matter

C40S2.text: In particular, in the early universe, ordinary matter was ionized and interacted strongly with radiation via Thomson scattering.
C40S2.title: Dark matter

C40S3.text: Dark matter does not interact directly with radiation, but it does affect the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by its gravitational potential (mainly on large scales) and by its effects on the density and velocity of ordinary matter.
C40S3.title: Dark matter

C40S4.text: Ordinary and dark matter perturbations, therefore, evolve differently with time and leave different imprints on the CMB.
C40S4.title: Dark matter

C49S2.text: This is also the reason why neutrinos, which move at nearly the speed of light and therefore would fall under hot dark matter, cannot make up the bulk of dark matter.
C49S2.title: Dark matter

C55S1.text: However, multiple lines of evidence suggest the majority of dark matter is not baryonic:
C55S1.title: Dark matter

C56S1.text: Sufficient diffuse, baryonic gas or dust would be visible when backlit by stars.
C56S1.title: Dark matter

C57S2.text: If there are more baryons, then there should also be more helium, lithium and heavier elements synthesized during the Big Bang.
C57S2.title: Dark matter

C57S4.text: In contrast, large-scale structure and other observations indicate that the total matter density is about 30% of the critical density.
C57S4.title: Dark matter

C59S1.text: Detailed analysis of the small irregularities (anisotropies) in the cosmic microwave background by WMAP and Planck indicate that around five-sixths of the total matter is in a form that only interacts significantly with ordinary matter or photons through gravitational effects.
C59S1.title: Dark matter

C60S1.text: There are two main candidates for non-baryonic dark matter: new particles and primordial black holes.
C60S1.title: Dark matter

C60S2.text: Unlike baryonic matter, nonbaryonic particles do not contribute to the formation of the elements in the early universe (Big Bang nucleosynthesis) and so its presence is felt only via its gravitational effects (such as weak lensing).
C60S2.title: Dark matter

C61S1.text: There exists no formal definition of a Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP), but broadly, it is an elementary particle which interacts via gravity and any other force (or forces) which is as weak as or weaker than the weak nuclear force, but also non-vanishing in strength.
C61S1.title: Dark matter

C61S2.text: Many WIMP candidates are expected to have been produced thermally in the early Universe, similarly to the particles of the Standard Model according to Big Bang cosmology, and usually will constitute cold dark matter.
C61S2.title: Dark matter

C62S1.text: Because supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics readily predict a new particle with these properties, this apparent coincidence has been called the "WIMP miracle", and a stable supersymmetric partner has long been a prime explanation for dark matter.
C62S1.title: Dark matter

C62S2.text: Experimental efforts to detect WIMPs include the search for products of WIMP annihilation, including gamma rays, neutrinos and cosmic rays in nearby galaxies and galaxy clusters; direct detection experiments designed to measure the collision of WIMPs with nuclei in the laboratory, as well as attempts to directly produce WIMPs in colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider at CERN.
C62S2.title: Dark matter

C62S3.text: In the early 2010s, results from direct-detection experiments along with the lack of evidence for supersymmetry at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiment have cast doubt on the simplest WIMP hypothesis.
C62S3.title: Dark matter

C63S1.text: Axions are hypothetical elementary particles originally theorized in 1978 independently by Frank Wilczek and Steven Weinberg as the Goldstone boson of Peccei–Quinn theory, which had been proposed in 1977 to solve the strong CP problem in quantum chromodynamics (QCD).
C63S1.title: Dark matter

C63S2.text: QCD effects produce an effective periodic potential in which the axion field moves.
C63S2.title: Dark matter

C63S3.text: Expanding the potential about one of its minima, one finds that the product of the axion mass with the axion decay constant is determined by the topological susceptibility of the QCD vacuum.
C63S3.title: Dark matter

C63S4.text: An axion with mass that is much less than 60 keV/c2 is long-lived and weakly interacting: a perfect dark matter candidate.
C63S4.title: Dark matter

C64S1.text: The oscillations of the axion field about the minimum of the effective potential, the so-called misalignment mechanism, generate a cosmological population of cold axions with an abundance depending on the mass of the axion.
C64S1.title: Dark matter

C64S2.text: With a mass above 5 μeV/c2 (10−11 times the electron mass) axions could account for dark matter, and thus be both a dark-matter candidate and a solution to the strong CP problem.
C64S2.title: Dark matter

C64S3.text: If inflation occurs at a low scale and lasts sufficiently long, the axion mass can be as low as 1 peV/c2.
C64S3.title: Dark matter

C71S1.text: Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothetical black holes that formed soon after the Big Bang.
C71S1.title: Dark matter

C71S2.text: In the inflationary era and early radiation-dominated universe, extremely dense pockets of subatomic matter may have been tightly packed to the point of gravitational collapse, creating black holes without the supernova compression typically needed to create stellar black holes.
C71S2.title: Dark matter

C71S3.text: The idea was first suggested by Yakov Zeldovich and Igor Dmitriyevich Novikov in 1966, and independently by Stephen Hawking in 1971.
C71S3.title: Dark matter

C71S4.text: Because PBHs would form prior to stellar evolution, they are non-baryonic dark matter candidates and are not limited to the narrow mass range of stellar black holes; they could range from Planck-mass relics to supermassive scales.
C71S4.title: Dark matter

C72S1.text: Interest in PBHs as a primary component of dark matter was revived following the 2015 discovery of gravitational waves by LIGO.
C72S1.title: Dark matter

C72S2.text: Their first detected merger involved black holes of approximately 30 solar masses; such objects are difficult to explain via standard stellar collapse but fit the predicted mass range for PBHs formed during the QCD transition in the early universe.
C72S2.title: Dark matter

C72S3.text: This interest was bolstered in November 2025, when the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA collaboration reported a candidate gravitational wave signal from a sub-solar mass merger.
C72S3.title: Dark matter

C72S4.text: As no astrophysical process is known to produce black holes below the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses), confirmed sub-solar mass objects would be strong evidence for a primordial origin.
C72S4.title: Dark matter

C72S5.text: As there have been no gravitational waves detected at z>1 (>6 Gya), and the sensitivity to lower-mass collisions falls off with distance, we are not currently able to detect collisions in the earliest half of the age of the universe.
C72S5.title: Dark matter

C73S1.text: Further support for the PBH hypothesis has emerged from James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the high-redshift universe (z > 7).
C73S1.title: Dark matter

C73S2.text: JWST discovered unexpected populations of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs, compact very high redshift objects) and "overmassive black hole galaxies" such as UHZ1 and GHZ2, which contain supermassive black holes appearing less than 500 million years after the Big Bang and outweighing their galaxy's stars.
C73S2.title: Dark matter

C73S3.text: These active galactic nuclei challenge standard models of accretion from "light" stellar black hole seeds, and suggest "heavy seeds" formed via direct collapse or PBHs, which could account for a significant fraction of dark matter halos.
C73S3.title: Dark matter

C74S1.text: Various observational constraints, such as gravitational microlensing data from the Subaru Telescope (HSC) and from Voyager 1 electron-positron data have ruled out PBHs constituting 100% of dark matter in specific mass windows (e.g., evaporating tiny black holes or monochromatic intermediate-mass populations).
C74S1.title: Dark matter

C75S3.text: Consequently, producing the required abundance of PBHs typically necessitates "exotic" inflation models, often featuring inflection points, bumps, or plateaus in the inflaton potential, which can amplify fluctuations by orders of magnitude.
C75S3.title: Dark matter

C75S4.text: Critics argue that these models require significant fine-tuning, as the resulting PBH abundance is exponentially sensitive to the amplitude of these fluctuations; meaning that a slight deviation in parameters results in either a negligible amount of dark matter or a universe dominated entirely by black holes.
C75S4.title: Dark matter

C76S1.text: by these exotic inflation models provide a unified explanation for observational anomalies seen by LIGO and JWST that particle models do not address.
C76S1.title: Dark matter

C77S2.text: One such mechanism is the QCD phase transition; as the universe cooled through this epoch, the reduction in the equation of state (pressure) naturally lowered the threshold for gravitational collapse.
C77S2.title: Dark matter

C77S3.text: This effect automatically enhances the formation of black holes at the solar mass scale, comparable to those detected by gravitational wave observatories, without requiring a precisely tuned peak in the inflation power spectrum.
C77S3.title: Dark matter

C77S4.text: Additionally, models involving multiple scalar fields can produce sharp spikes in density fluctuations through dynamic interactions, such as rapid turns in the field trajectory, which derive the necessary conditions from the model's geometric structure rather than from fine-tuned parameters.
C77S4.title: Dark matter

C87S1.text: Indirect detection experiments search for the products of the self-annihilation or decay of dark matter particles in outer space.
C87S1.title: Dark matter

C87S2.text: For example, in regions of high dark matter density (e.g., the centre of the Milky Way) two dark matter particles could annihilate to produce gamma rays or Standard Model particle–antiparticle pairs.
C87S2.title: Dark matter

C87S3.text: Alternatively, if a dark matter particle is unstable, it could decay into Standard Model (or other) particles.
C87S3.title: Dark matter

C87S4.text: These processes could be detected indirectly through an excess of gamma rays, antiprotons or positrons emanating from high density regions in the Milky Way and other galaxies.
C87S4.title: Dark matter

C88S1.text: A few of the dark matter particles passing through the Sun or Earth may scatter off atoms and lose energy.
C88S1.title: Dark matter

C88S2.text: Thus dark matter may accumulate at the center of these bodies, increasing the chance of collision/annihilation.
C88S2.title: Dark matter

C88S3.text: This could produce a distinctive signal in the form of high-energy neutrinos.
C88S3.title: Dark matter

C88S4.text: Such a signal would be strong indirect proof of WIMP dark matter.
C88S4.title: Dark matter

C88S5.text: High-energy neutrino telescopes such as AMANDA, IceCube and ANTARES are searching for this signal.
C88S5.title: Dark matter

C89S1.text: The Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope observed more gamma rays in 2008 than expected from the Milky Way, but scientists concluded this was most likely due to incorrect estimation of the telescope's sensitivity.
C89S1.title: Dark matter

C90S1.text: The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope is searching for similar gamma rays.
C90S1.title: Dark matter

C90S2.text: In 2009, an as yet unexplained surplus of gamma rays from the Milky Way's galactic center was found in Fermi data.
C90S2.title: Dark matter

C90S3.text: This Galactic Center GeV excess might be due to dark matter annihilation or to a population of pulsars.
C90S3.title: Dark matter

C90S4.text: In April 2012, an analysis of previously available data from Fermi's Large Area Telescope instrument produced statistical evidence of a 130 GeV signal in the gamma radiation coming from the center of the Milky Way.
C90S4.title: Dark matter

C90S5.text: WIMP annihilation was seen as the most probable explanation.
C90S5.title: Dark matter

C91S1.text: At higher energies, ground-based gamma-ray telescopes have set limits on the annihilation of dark matter in dwarf spheroidal galaxies and in clusters of galaxies.
C91S1.title: Dark matter

C92S2.text: They could be from dark matter annihilation or from pulsars.
C92S2.title: Dark matter

C93S1.text: In 2013, results from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on the International Space Station indicated excess high-energy cosmic rays which could be due to dark matter annihilation.
C93S1.title: Dark matter

C94S1.text: The detection by LIGO in September 2015 of gravitational waves opens the possibility of observing dark matter in a new way, particularly if it is in the form of primordial black holes.
C94S1.title: Dark matter

C95S1.text: Beyond searching for annihilation products, astrophysicists are using celestial objects as natural detectors to constrain dark matter particle properties.
C95S1.title: Dark matter

C96S1.text: Stellar heating: If dark matter particles capture inside dense stars like neutron stars or white dwarfs, they can deposit kinetic energy during the capture process or through subsequent annihilation.
C96S1.title: Dark matter

C96S2.text: This mechanism, known as "dark kinetic heating", would maintain the star at a temperature higher than expected for its age, potentially arresting its cooling indefinitely.
C96S2.title: Dark matter

C96S3.text: The observation of old, "cold" neutron stars therefore places stringent limits on the scattering cross-section of dark matter particles with nucleons, as any significant interaction would have kept these stars hotter than observed.
C96S3.title: Dark matter

C106S1.text: If dark matter is not an undiscovered particle, then the next possibility is that general relativity, the theory underpinning modern cosmology, is incorrect.
C106S1.title: Dark matter

C106S2.text: General relativity is well-tested on Solar System scales, but its validity on galactic or cosmological scales has not been well proven.
C106S2.title: Dark matter

C106S3.text: A suitable modification to general relativity can conceivably eliminate the need for dark matter.
C106S3.title: Dark matter

C106S4.text: The best-known theories of this class are modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) and its relativistic generalization tensor–vector–scalar gravity (TeVeS), f(R) gravity, negative mass, dark fluid, entropic gravity, conformal gravity, and massive gravity.
C106S4.title: Dark matter

C107S1.text: A problem with modifying gravity is that observational evidence for dark matter – let alone general relativity – comes from so many independent approaches (see § Observational evidence above).
C107S1.title: Dark matter

C107S2.text: Explaining any individual observation is possible but explaining all of them in the absence of dark matter is very difficult.
C107S2.title: Dark matter

C107S3.text: Nonetheless, there have been some scattered successes for alternative hypotheses, such as a 2016 test of gravitational lensing in entropic gravity and a 2020 measurement of a unique MOND effect.
C107S3.title: Dark matter

C107S4.text: The prevailing opinion among most astrophysicists is that while modifications to general relativity can conceivably explain part of the observational evidence, there is probably enough data to conclude there must be some form of dark matter present in the universe.
C107S4.title: Dark matter

C108S1.text: While WIMPs, axions, and primordial black holes remain the primary candidates for dark matter, numerous other theories have been proposed to address specific observational anomalies or theoretical motivations.
C108S1.title: Dark matter

C182S1.text: In astronomy and cosmology, baryonic dark matter is hypothetical dark matter composed of baryons.
C182S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C182S2.text: Only a small proportion of the dark matter in the universe is likely to be baryonic.
C182S2.title: Baryonic dark matter

C183S1.text: As "dark matter", baryonic dark matter is undetectable by its emitted radiation, but its presence can be inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter.
C183S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C183S2.text: This form of dark matter is composed of "baryons", heavy subatomic particles such as protons and neutrons and combinations of these, including non-emitting ordinary atoms.
C183S2.title: Baryonic dark matter

C184S1.text: Baryonic dark matter may occur in non-luminous gas or in Massive Astrophysical Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs) – condensed objects such as black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs, very faint stars, or non-luminous objects like planets and brown dwarfs.
C184S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C185S1.text: The total amount of baryonic dark matter can be inferred from models of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and observations of the cosmic microwave background.
C185S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C185S2.text: Both indicate that the amount of baryonic dark matter is much smaller than the total amount of dark matter.
C185S2.title: Baryonic dark matter

C186S1.text: From the perspective of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, a larger amount of ordinary (baryonic) matter implies a denser early universe, more efficient conversion of matter to helium-4, and less unburned deuterium remaining.
C186S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C186S2.text: If all of the dark matter in the universe were baryonic, then there would be much less deuterium in the universe than is observed.
C186S2.title: Baryonic dark matter

C186S3.text: This could be resolved if more deuterium were somehow generated, but large efforts in the 1970s failed to identify plausible mechanisms for this to occur.
C186S3.title: Baryonic dark matter

C186S4.text: For instance, MACHOs, which include, for example, brown dwarfs (bodies of hydrogen and helium with masses less than 0.08 M☉ or 1.6×1029 kg), never begin nuclear fusion of hydrogen, but they do burn deuterium.
C186S4.title: Baryonic dark matter

C186S5.text: Other possibilities that were examined include "Jupiters", which are similar to brown dwarfs but have masses ∼ {\displaystyle \sim } 0.001 M☉ (2
C186S5.title: Baryonic dark matter

C187S1.text: ×1027 kg) and do not burn anything, and white dwarfs.
C187S1.title: Baryonic dark matter

C189S1.text: Biological dark matter is an informal term for unclassified or poorly understood genetic material.
C189S1.title: Biological dark matter

C189S2.text: This genetic material may refer to genetic material produced by unclassified microorganisms.
C189S2.title: Biological dark matter

C189S3.text: By extension, biological dark matter may also refer to the un-isolated microorganisms whose existence can only be inferred from the genetic material that they produce.
C189S3.title: Biological dark matter

C189S4.text: Some of the genetic material may not fall under the three existing domains of life: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota; thus, it has been suggested that a possible fourth domain of life may yet be discovered, although other explanations are also probable.
C189S4.title: Biological dark matter

C189S5.text: Alternatively, the genetic material may refer to non-coding DNA (so-called "junk DNA") and non-coding RNA produced by known organisms.
C189S5.title: Biological dark matter

C190S1.text: Much of the genomic dark matter is thought to originate from ancient transposable elements and from other low-complexity repetitive elements.
C190S1.title: Biological dark matter

C190S2.text: Uncategorized genetic material is found in humans and many other species.
C190S2.title: Biological dark matter

C190S3.text: Their phylogenetic novelty could indicate the cellular organisms or viruses from which they evolved.
C190S3.title: Biological dark matter

C191S1.text: Up to 99% of all living microorganisms cannot be cultured, so few functional insights exist about the metabolic potential of these organisms.
C191S1.title: Biological dark matter

C192S1.text: Sequences that are believed to be derived from unknown microbes are referred to as the microbial dark matter, the dark virome, or dark matter fungi.
C192S1.title: Biological dark matter

C192S3.text: It has been estimated that in material from humans, between 40 and 90% of viral sequences are from dark matter.
C192S3.title: Biological dark matter

C192S4.text: Human blood contains over three thousand different DNA sequences which cannot yet be identified.
C192S4.title: Biological dark matter

C192S5.text: A mycological study from 2023 found that dark matter fungi seem to dominate the fungal kingdom.
C192S5.title: Biological dark matter

C194S1.title: Biological dark matter

C195S1.text: In February 2023, scientists reported the findings of unusual DNA strands from the microorganisms in the "dark microbiome" in the Atacama Desert, the driest non-polar desert on Earth.
